sections.body: (p. 133) No text is printed under this heading; see 9.1.1 Plans, Specifications and Estimates and 9.1.2 Structural Fills.
key_points: Design-bid-build construction documents: plans, specifications and estimates (9.1.1) and structural fills (9.1.2)
sections.applicability: General guidance on construction document preparation for shallow foundation projects.

sections.title: Plans, Specifications and Estimates
sections.summary: Plans show footing locations, dimensions, reinforcement, elevations, embedment and backfill, usually with a foundation data sheet of subsurface data; the geotechnical report should be available to contractors. Abutment backfill must be well compacted and not lose fines (filters or geocomposite drains), with drainage details. FHWA (1996) Sections 208, 209, 552 and 554 apply; special provisions cover soil/rock treatment, ground water control and special shoring. Pay items are listed.
sections.body: (pp. 133-134) Plans are typically developed to show footing locations, dimensions and details for steel reinforcement, required footing elevations, and the embedment and backfill dimensions. A foundation data sheet is usually provided to show summary subsurface data in spatial relation to the foundations; material descriptions, ground water levels, SPT data and other subsurface information are particularly valuable to the contractor for evaluating excavation, shoring, dewatering and other construction details usually left to the contractor to design or select. The geotechnical report should be made available to contractors. The plans should detail the drainage and backfill requirements for abutments and retaining walls. For bridges the abutment area is critical because it performs many functions: to prevent the notorious 'bump at the end of the bridge' the abutment backfill must be properly compacted and not prone to material loss by migration of fine-grained material (materials that promote good compaction: Soils and Foundations Workshop Reference Manual, Cheney & Chassie, 2000); underdrain filter material or prefabricated geocomposite drains can be specified to prevent fine-grained soil migration, and drainage details should prevent build-up of pore water pressures behind the stemwall. Specifications typically include requirements for concrete, steel reinforcement and construction procedures. The FHWA Standard Specifications (FHWA, 1996) include Section 208, Structure Excavation and Backfill for Selected Major Structures; Section 209, Structure Excavation and Backfill; Section 552, Structural Concrete; and Section 554, Reinforcing Steel. They cover material requirements, preparation and compaction of a suitable bearing level in soil or rock, temporary cut slopes and shoring, shop drawings, protection of foundation conditions during construction, concrete delivery and placement, curing and acceptance. The specifications should reference the availability of the geotechnical report. Special provisions might be necessary where special foundation soil/rock treatment or ground water control is required; soft or liquefiable foundation soils may need special treatment to develop firm foundation conditions, and tight, sensitive areas such as next to existing structure foundations might need special shoring requirements. Pay items may include Structure Excavation, Foundation Fill, Structural Backfill, Shoring and Bracing, and Cofferdams; the footings may be incidental to structure construction, or concrete and steel may be measured and paid by unit quantities and prices.
key_points: Plans show footing locations, dimensions, reinforcement, elevations, embedment and backfill dimensions
A foundation data sheet usually shows summary subsurface data in spatial relation to the foundations
Geotechnical report should be made available to contractors and referenced in the specifications
Abutment backfill must be properly compacted and not prone to loss of fines, to prevent the 'bump at the end of the bridge'
Underdrain filter material or prefabricated geocomposite drains can prevent fine-grained soil migration; drainage details prevent pore pressure behind the stemwall
FHWA Standard Specifications (1996): Sections 208 and 209 (structure excavation and backfill), 552 (structural concrete), 554 (reinforcing steel)
Special provisions for soil/rock treatment, ground water control, soft or liquefiable soils, and shoring next to existing foundations
Pay items: Structure Excavation, Foundation Fill, Structural Backfill, Shoring and Bracing, Cofferdams; footings incidental or paid by unit quantities
sections.applicability: Preparing plans, specifications and pay items for shallow foundation construction contracts.

sections.title: Structural Fills
sections.summary: A compacted structural fill supporting a bridge abutment needs special details and specifications; Figure 9-1 (after Cheney & Chassie, 2000) shows the zones of select structural fill (100% T99) and highway embankment material (95% and 90% T180), the 1.5-m select pad beneath abutment footings and the berm geometry. The select material specification and the Washington, Nevada and Michigan structural fill specifications are in Appendix A. Unsuitable or deleterious material (peat, muck, wood, organic waste, coal, charcoal) is prohibited.
sections.body: (p. 134) Special details and specifications are necessary when constructing a compacted structural fill to support a bridge foundation such as an abutment. Figure 9-1 (adapted from Cheney and Chassie, 2000) shows recommended details for construction of a structural approach embankment, including zones of specified materials and compaction requirements. The materials specifications are chosen to provide a firm, non-yielding condition suitable for bridge abutment spread footing support. The specification for select material is from the Soils and Foundations Workshop Reference Manual (Cheney & Chassie, 2000) and is included in Appendix A. Specifications from Washington, Nevada, and Michigan DOTs for structural fills beneath spread footing abutments are also in Appendix A. Select structural fill and highway embankment material should not include unsuitable material such as peat, muck, wood, organic waste, coal, charcoal, or any other deleterious material.
key_points: Structural fill specifications are critical for bridge abutment spread footing support
Figure 9-1 shows recommended structural approach embankment details
Three zones: Select Structural Fill (100% compaction T99), Highway Embankment 150mm topsize (95% T180), Highway Embankment (90% T180)
1.5 m pad of select material placed beneath abutments on spread footings
Embankment placed to the line shown before abutment construction or pile driving; Figure 9-1 marks a 15 m (50 ft) minimum dimension
Highway embankment and select material placed simultaneously at the vertical payment line (Note 1)
Unsuitable materials (peat, muck, wood, organic waste, coal, charcoal) must be excluded
State DOT specifications (WA, NV, MI) for structural fills are in Appendix A
figures: Figure 9-1: Structural Approach Fill Details (after Cheney & Chassie, 2000): zones of Select Structural Fill (minimum 100% compaction, T99), Highway Embankment Material with 150 mm (6 in) maximum topsize (minimum 95% compaction, T180) and Highway Embankment Material (minimum 90% compaction, T180); 1.5 m (5 ft) pad of select material beneath abutments on spread footings; minimum berm/end slope breakpoint 0.6 m (2 ft) above the top of the footing and 1.2 m (4 ft) out from the front edge; a 15 m (50 ft) minimum dimension beside 'place embankment to this line prior to abutment construction or pile driving'; a 3 (min) to 1 slope; backfill to a point 1.5 m (5 ft) behind the wingwall; Note 1: highway embankment and select material placed simultaneously 'of the vertical payment line' (as printed) (p. 135)
sections.applicability: Specifying structural fill materials and compaction requirements for bridge abutments on spread footings.

sections.title: Design-Build Procurement
sections.summary: Design-build projects require owner-provided Geotechnical Data Report (GDR) with sufficient information for foundation design. Geotechnical Interpretive and Baseline Reports reduce bidding uncertainty and risk. Special Provisions should include design criteria, settlement and scour criteria, seismic criteria, and a QC/QA submittal process.
sections.body: (p. 134) The design-build procurement approach should include owner-provided geotechnical data sufficient for foundation design. A Geotechnical Data Report (GDR) is recommended, and Geotechnical Interpretive Reports and Geotechnical Baseline Reports may also be prepared to document expected surface and subsurface conditions, reduce uncertainty during bidding, and reduce risk contingencies. The GDR should identify special conditions affecting structural fill and shallow foundation design/construction and provide test results for necessary geotechnical properties. Because alignment and structure locations may not be fixed in design-build procurement, the contractor may need to provide supplemental explorations and testing. Special Provision specifications should include requirements for codified design criteria, tolerable settlement criteria, estimated scour depths, seismic criteria, adherence to standard specifications, and a submittal and review process with minimum quality control and assurance plan.
key_points: Design-build procurement should include owner-provided geotechnical data (GDR recommended)
Geotechnical Interpretive Reports and Baseline Reports reduce bidding uncertainty and risk
GDR should identify special conditions and provide necessary geotechnical test results
Contractor may need supplemental explorations if alignment/structure locations are not fixed
Special Provisions should include: design criteria, settlement criteria, scour depths, seismic criteria
Submittal and review process with QC/QA plan should be prescribed
Specifications should impose contractor requirements to achieve desired foundation performance
sections.applicability: Preparing geotechnical documents and specifications for design-build shallow foundation projects.
